title: Granular KV tiering and lazy GPU-commit prototype
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Prototype a multi-granularity paged/blocked KV cache that minimizes GPU memcpy churn under oversubscription by combining thin-slab prefetching, lazy GPU-commit semantics, and a resident-set budgeting allocator. Goal is to reduce per-token memcpy overhead and lower P99 latency tail when many short contexts contend for limited GPU-residency, while preserving correctness for continuous batching and KV cache reuse across requests.

Motivation:
- Current slab/paged designs either commit full slabs to GPU eagerly (causing high memcpy overhead) or perform coarse-grained eviction that increases re-materialization when prefixes are reused.
- Continuous batching amplifies the cost: many concurrent requests bring partial prefixes with high temporal locality; naive commits lead to GPU oversubscription and spikes in latency.

Proposal (high level):
1) Multi-granularity blocks: implement two block sizes mapped in the cache metadata: superblocks (~64KB) for low-overhead residency accounting and thin slabs (~4KB) for fine-grained prefetch/eviction. Metadata is a compact block map (bitsets + LRU cohorts) that supports atomic promotions from thin-slab -> superblock.
2) Thin-slab prefetching: when a request forecasts token consumption beyond a threshold (tokens_remaining > T_prefetch and observed reuse score > S), schedule thin-slab async pinned-host -> GPU memcpy for only the needed thin slabs. This uses CUDA streams (or analogous APIs) to overlap with compute.
3) Lazy GPU-commit: defer final GPU residency promotion until either (a) the thin-slab copy completes and an execution token is reached, or (b) a hotness validator marks the slab as persistently hot (usage_count > H). Until then keep the slab in a pinned host staging area that the runtime can read from if needed (slow path).
4) Resident-budget allocator: maintain a budget per-GPU in units of superblocks. Thin slabs reserve ephemeral sub-budgets that do not immediately count against the hard budget until promoted. Eviction prefers least-recently-used thin slabs within superblocks, then whole superblocks.
5) Batch-aware hotness scoring: integrate with continuous batching to assign hotness scores based on prefix reuse within the current batch window, end-to-end latency contribution, and KV lifetime estimates coming from the tokenizer/profiled sequences.
6) Fallback and graceful degradation: when budget exhausted, fall back to pinned-host streaming reads with backpressure into the batcher (limit concurrent pinned reads) and optionally route small requests to a smaller model variant pinned in GPU to preserve SLOs.

Implementation details & trade-offs:
- Metadata layout: keep block map as flat arrays of 32-bit words to ensure atomic updates without locks on the hot path. Use per-GPU epoch counters to avoid ABA problems during eviction.
- Prefetch heuristics: conservative defaults (T_prefetch=12 tokens, S=0.25 reuse score) to avoid unnecessary memcopies; these are tunable by workloads and exposed in Optimize recommendations.
- Lazy commit correctness: lazy commit adds complexity for concurrent writers (model KV writes during generation). Use a small write buffer and write-through semantics for token writes that update KV; promotion requires a short handoff that synchronizes pending writes. This approach favors correctness over absolute minimal latency but reduces memcpy volume.
- Continuous batching integration: the batch scheduler will annotate entries with expected sequence length and reuse probability so cache manager can make prefetch decisions per-request in a batch. This requires modest API extension between scheduler and cache manager (added field: expected_remaining_tokens).

Acceptance criteria:
- Functional: no correctness regressions; tokens generated must match baseline for pinned-read slow-path and promoted fast-path.
- Perf: under 2x oversubscription test (2x logical working set vs GPU-resident capacity), reduce total device memcpy bytes by >=20% and improve throughput by >=8% on target workloads (long-tail conversation + many short prefix reuse).
- Latency: p99 generation latency under experimental load must not regress >2% compared to current runtime when promotion threshold tuned for production defaults.
- Stability: pass stress tests (24h mixed traffic), and OOM recovery path validated (eviction and fallback works without crashes).

Rollout plan:
1) Merge prototype behind feature flag + unit/integration tests.
2) Canary on staging: 5% of traffic for 48h and collect metrics (memcpy bytes, throughput, p50/p95/p99).
3) Run targeted A/B with oversubscription test harness for workload families (chatty small-context vs long-form).
4) Ramp to production canary 25% then 100% with telemetry and automated rollback on SLA triggers.

Backward compatibility and observability:
- Default feature flag off; Optimize will recommend enabling for oversubscribed workloads.
- Expose metrics: thin_slab_prefetches, lazy_promotions, pinned_host_reads, superblock_evictions, bytes_memcpy_gpu, avg_promotion_latency. Add per-request annotation in tracing for cache hits/misses.

Open questions / Risks:
- Fine-tuning thresholds (T_prefetch, H) across diverse workloads; risk of under-prefetch causing compute stalls. Plan: run sweep experiments and ship auto-tuning in Optimize.
- Additional complexity in write-path concurrency may introduce subtle bugs. Plan: add fuzzer tests for concurrent read/write/promote patterns.
- Memory fragmentation from mix of sizes; mitigation: periodic compaction of thin slabs into contiguous superblocks during low-load windows.

Link to detailed design doc and draft PR attached in attachments.

Next steps (this ticket):
- Complete runtime metadata primitives and write-through handoff (owner: Mateo).
- Add scheduler->cache API extension and basic hotness estimator (owner: Claire Zhang, infra).
- Benchmarks: create oversubscription harness and baseline measurements (owner: SRE team).
